body.statement:
For every \((G,T,e)\in\mathcal G_{n,k}\) with \(d_e(G)<\infty\),
\[
 d_e(G)
 \leq \vartheta_{n-1,\,|D|-n+2}
 \leq \vartheta_{n-1,\,k+1}.
\]
More precisely,
\[
 d_e(G)\leq\min\!\left\{2^{|D|-n+2},\tau_{n-1}\right\},
 \qquad
 \vartheta_{n-1,k+1}\leq\min\!\left\{2^{k+1},\tau_{n-1}\right\}.
\]
These inequalities hold even when the full generic parameter fiber is positive dimensional.  Consequently,
\[
 D_k(n)\leq\vartheta_{n-1,k+1}\leq\min\!\left\{2^{k+1},\tau_{n-1}\right\}.
\]
For six vertices this yields
\[
 D_2(6)\leq6,\qquad D_3(6)\leq8,\qquad D_4(6)\leq12,
 \qquad D_k(6)\leq24\quad\text{for every admissible }k\geq5.
\]
body.justification: This gives a universal projection-aware ceiling that couples the available child-block count with the query component's cycle rank.
body.gap: Tree-only identification theory and old higher-degree small SEM examples do not provide this single-coordinate joint vertex/cycle-rank bound.
body.consumer: The result supplies the sharpest proved theoretical ambiguity budget, including the six-vertex caps \(6,8,12,24\); the fixed-parameter dispatcher retains its efficiently available size-binomial cap.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \((G,T,e)\in\mathcal G_{n,k}\) and suppose \(d_e(G)<\infty\).  Then \(\lambda_e\) is algebraic over \(K_G\) by the definition of \(d_e\).  Multiplying the defining covariance identity on the left by \((I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\) and on the right by \(I_n-\Lambda\) gives
\[
 \Omega=(I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(I_n-\Lambda).
\tag{1}
\]
Thus every disturbance coordinate lies in \(K_G(\lambda_D)\).  The reverse inclusion of generators is immediate from \(K_G\subseteq L\) and \(\lambda_D\subseteq L\), so
\[
 L=K_G(\lambda_D).
\tag{2}
\]

Choose \(U\subseteq\lambda_D\setminus\{\lambda_e\}\) maximal algebraically independent over \(K_G\), put \(F=K_G(U)\), and enumerate
\[
 y=(y_1,\ldots,y_q)=\lambda_D\setminus U.
\]
Because \(\lambda_e\) is algebraic over \(K_G\), it cannot enlarge the algebraically independent set \(U\).  Maximality of \(U\), followed by adjoining the finitely many coordinates in \(y\), therefore makes \(L/F\) finite.  It is separable because \(F\) has characteristic zero.  The minimal polynomial \(p(t)\in K_G[t]\) of \(\lambda_e\) remains irreducible over \(F=K_G(U)\).  Indeed, a nontrivial factorization over \(K_G(U)\) could be cleared of its finitely many denominators; because \(U\) is algebraically independent and the infinite field \(K_G\) contains \(\mathbb C\), one could then specialize \(U\) to a point of \(K_G^{|U|}\) where all denominators and both leading coefficients are nonzero.  The specialization would be a nontrivial factorization of \(p\) in \(K_G[t]\), a contradiction.  Consequently
\[
 [F(\lambda_e):F]=[K_G(\lambda_e):K_G]=d_e(G).
\tag{3}
\]

By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) and \(\mathrm{def:generic\mbox{-}fiber}\), localizing first at \(S_G\) and then at the nonzero elements of \(K_G[U]\) gives an evaluation homomorphism
\[
 F[y_1,\ldots,y_q]\longrightarrow L
\]
whose kernel is generated by the missing-bidirected residuals \(F_{ij}\).  If \(g_a\in F[t]\) is the minimal polynomial of \(y_a\), there are polynomials \(c_{a,ij}\in F[y]\) such that
\[
 g_a(y_a)=\sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}c_{a,ij}(y)F_{ij}(y).
\tag{4}
\]
Differentiate (4) and evaluate in \(L\).  Since every residual vanishes, this gives
\[
 g_a'(y_a)\,dy_a
 =\sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}c_{a,ij}(y)\,dF_{ij}.
\tag{5}
\]
Separability gives \(g_a'(y_a)\ne0\), so the evaluated residual gradients span all \(dy_a\).  The residual Jacobian with respect to \(y\) therefore has rank \(q\).  Select residuals \(f_1,\ldots,f_q\) with nonzero Jacobian determinant \(\Delta\in L\).

There are exactly \(d_e(G)\) distinct \(F\)-embeddings of \(F(\lambda_e)\) into an algebraic closure \(\overline F\), by (3) and separability.  Each extends to an \(F\)-embedding of the finite algebraic extension \(L/F\): adjoin the remaining algebraic generators one at a time and, at each step, send the next generator to any root in \(\overline F\) of the transported minimal polynomial.  Every extension is a common zero of \(f_1,\ldots,f_q\), and it sends the nonzero field element \(\Delta\) to a nonzero element.  It is therefore a nonsingular isolated zero of the selected square system.  Embeddings with different restrictions to \(F(\lambda_e)\) have distinct \(\lambda_e\)-coordinates.

Partition the variables \(y\) into nonempty blocks indexed by their child vertices, and let \(r_v\) be the size of block \(v\).  Then
\[
 1\leq r_v\leq\operatorname{indeg}_D(v).
\tag{6}
\]
The displayed formula for \(F_{ij}\) is affine-linear in each of the two child blocks indexed by \(i,j\).  Thus a selected residual meeting one remaining block is unary, and one meeting two remaining blocks is bilinear with multidegree at most one in each block.  Decompose the equation-block incidence graph of the selected square system into connected components.  A nonzero monomial in \(\Delta\) supplies a row-to-column matching, so each component contains equally many equations and variables.

Consider the component containing \(\lambda_e\).  Suppose it contains \(b\) variable blocks, \(u\) unary equations, and \(m_H\) binary equations.  If \(b>1\), the binary equations form a connected simple graph \(H\) on the blocks: connectivity follows from the choice of component, and simplicity follows because there is only one residual for an unordered pair of distinct child vertices.  If \(b=1\), take \(H\) to be the one-vertex graph.  Since the component is square,
\[
 \sum_{v\in V(H)}r_v=u+m_H.
\tag{7}
\]

The multihomogeneous bound \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\) bounds the number of isolated zeros of this component by the coefficient of \(\prod_vX_v^{r_v}\) in
\[
 \left(\prod_{\ell=1}^{u}X_{v(\ell)}\right)
 \left(\prod_{\{v,w\}\in E(H)}(X_v+X_w)\right).
\tag{8}
\]
After subtracting the fixed unary exponents, (8) is \(c_H(s)\) for one prescribed nonnegative indegree vector \(s\); if a coordinate of \(s\) is negative, the coefficient is zero and cannot bound the already exhibited solutions, so the relevant coefficient has \(s\geq0\).  Every conjugate of \(\lambda_e\) supplies a distinct isolated zero in this component.  Hence
\[
 d_e(G)\leq c_H(s).
\tag{9}
\]

A finite acyclic directed graph has a source: otherwise repeatedly following an incoming arrow would repeat a vertex and create a directed cycle.  The root of the supplied arborescence has no incoming directed edge, since an arrow into it together with its tree path to the arrow's tail would create a cycle.  In particular at least one vertex has no nonempty child block, so
\[
 b\leq n-1.
\tag{10}
\]
Write \(g_H=m_H-b+1\) when \(b>1\), and set \(g_H=0\) when \(b=1\).  For \(b>1\), (6)--(7) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 g_H
 &=\sum_{v\in V(H)}r_v-u-b+1\\
 &\leq\sum_{v\in V(H)}\bigl(\operatorname{indeg}_D(v)-1\bigr)+1\\
 &\leq\sum_{v\ne\operatorname{root}(T)}
       \bigl(\operatorname{indeg}_D(v)-1\bigr)+1\\
 &=|D|-n+2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
The second inequality uses \(\mathrm{ass:arborescence}\): every nonroot vertex has one incoming tree arrow, so each omitted summand is nonnegative, while the root has indegree zero as just proved.  For \(b=1\), \(g_H=0\leq |D|-n+2\), because \(T\subseteq D\) and \(|T|=n-1\).  Thus (9)--(11) and \(\mathrm{def:joint\mbox{-}orientation\mbox{-}frontier}\) yield
\[
 d_e(G)\leq\vartheta_{n-1,\,|D|-n+2}.
\tag{12}
\]

Because \(T\subseteq D\) and \(|T|=n-1\), the excess-budget assumption gives
\[
 |D|-n+2=|D\setminus T|+1\leq k+1.
\tag{13}
\]
Monotonicity and \(\mathrm{lem:joint\mbox{-}orientation\mbox{-}frontier}\) now give
\[
 d_e(G)
 \leq\vartheta_{n-1,\,|D|-n+2}
 \leq\vartheta_{n-1,k+1}
 \leq\min\{2^{k+1},\tau_{n-1}\},
\tag{14}
\]
and applying the same lemma before (13) gives
\[
 d_e(G)\leq\min\{2^{|D|-n+2},\tau_{n-1}\}.
\tag{15}
\]
Maximizing (12)--(14) over all finite-degree members of \(\mathcal G_{n,k}\) proves
\[
 D_k(n)\leq\vartheta_{n-1,k+1}.
\tag{16}
\]
No step required the other components of the generic fiber to be zero-dimensional.

For \(n=6\), the exact recurrence table in \(\mathrm{lem:joint\mbox{-}orientation\mbox{-}frontier}\) gives
\[
 \vartheta_{5,3}=6,\qquad
 \vartheta_{5,4}=8,\qquad
 \vartheta_{5,5}=12,\qquad
 \vartheta_{5,g}=24\quad(g\geq6).
\]
Substitution of \(g=k+1\) into (16) proves
\[
 D_2(6)\leq6,\qquad D_3(6)\leq8,\qquad D_4(6)\leq12,
 \qquad D_k(6)\leq24\quad(k\geq5),
\]
for every admissible \(k\).
